screens.title: Spatial Audio & Audio Zones
screens.narratorSegment: Spatial audio is the perception that a sound comes from a particular place in 3D space, including its direction and distance. When you set Spatial Blend to full 3D you get basic positional cues, but true environmental realism comes from audio zones and reverb. An Audio Reverb Zone applies a reverb effect to any audio that plays inside its collider, simulating a cave, hall, or small room without changing the source clips. For example, place an Audio Reverb Zone inside a cavern and tune the reverb decay and wet level; footsteps and distant echoes will suddenly feel correct. A common misconception is to bake reverb into clips or duplicate clips per area; this becomes hard to manage. Using zones keeps source clips clean and lets you adjust acoustics globally. In practice you will combine zones with 3D rolloff curves and Max Distance to control how sources fade. As you test, listen for sudden jumps when crossing zone boundaries; smoothing or overlapping zones can avoid audible pops. Consider how music and dialogue thread through these spaces so the player experiences a consistent sound field. What space in your level would benefit most from a reverb zone?

keyIdea.title: Why Zones
keyIdea.text: Audio Reverb Zones let you change acoustic character per area without modifying individual clips, making environments feel authentic and adjustable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Spatial Audio & Audio Zones
Definition

Audio Reverb Zones

Zones apply environmental effects to any audio within their bounds. Use colliders as the trigger volume and tune reverb parameters in the zone inspector.

Use case
A cavern zone adds long decay and low dampening so echoes feel distant and atmospheric.
Best practice
  • Keep source clips dry; apply ambience via zones for flexibility.
  • Overlap zones slightly to avoid hard transitions.
  • Tune rolloff curves and Max Distance for consistent loudness.
Common mistake
Embedding reverb in clips makes global changes tedious and inconsistent across areas.
Example
Cave Scenario

Place a Box Collider as an Audio Reverb Zone around a cave. Set reverb decay high and wet level moderate. When the player crosses the trigger, footsteps and ambient wind will gain echo and warmth.

Parameter
Decay: long
Effect
Wet reverb on all sources inside
Key Takeaway

Zones let you control room acoustics per area, keeping source audio clean and adaptable.

screens.title: Occlusion & Obstruction
screens.narratorSegment: Occlusion and obstruction simulate how objects affect sound reaching the listener. Occlusion mutes or muffles a source when a complete or substantial barrier exists between listener and source. Obstruction models partial blocking, reducing high frequencies and slightly lowering volume. A common implementation starts with a raycast from the Audio Listener to the Audio Source. If the ray hits geometry, you treat it as occluded and adjust parameters—typically reduce volume and increase low-pass filtering. For partial hits or multiple rays, blend between unobstructed and obstructed states to avoid popping. For example, when the player stands behind a thin wall, apply a mild low-pass cutoff at around 2000 to 5000 hertz and reduce volume by a few decibels; for a concrete wall you may drop the cutoff lower and attenuate more. Remember that precise numbers depend on the game's sonic design. Test with music and SFX to ensure speech remains intelligible when intended. A misconception is using only distance rolloff; occlusion requires additional geometry checks to sound believable. The final step is smoothing parameter changes over time so transitions feel natural rather than abrupt.

keyIdea.text: Use raycasts from listener to source and smooth parameter changes to model occlusion and obstruction effectively.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Occlusion & Obstruction
Process

Raycast-based Occlusion

  1. Cast a ray from the Audio Listener to the Audio Source each update or on position changes.
  2. If the ray hits geometry, classify as occluded or partially obstructed.
  3. Adjust volume and set a low-pass cutoff parameter exposed on the mixer or source.
  4. Smooth changes over 100–300ms to avoid pops when entering/exiting occlusion.
Tuning hints
Use multiple rays for wide sources, or sample several points on a mesh when accuracy matters. Blend the filter values rather than snapping.
Example
Imagine a firefight occurring behind a metal door. A single raycast hits the door and you set the SFX group's low-pass cutoff to 1500Hz and reduce volume by 6dB. For a partially open door you lerp to 4000Hz and -3dB. Smooth transitions avoid noticeable jumps as doors open or players move.
Obstruction
Partial attenuation + mild low-pass
Occlusion
Stronger attenuation + lower cutoff
Key Takeaway

Raycasts plus smooth parameter blending give believable occlusion without heavy per-source CPU cost.

screens.title: Audio Mixer Effects
screens.narratorSegment: The Audio Mixer is Unity's central tool for grouping audio and applying effects. Each group can host effects such as Reverb, Echo, Distortion, Chorus, Flange, Delay, and lowpass/highpass filters. These effects change the character of sounds in ways that are expensive to simulate per-source but economical when done on groups. For instance, applying a low-pass filter to the SFX group can make all group sounds behave as if heard through water or behind a wall. A frequent misconception is assuming that effects on the master group are always cheaper; sometimes a well-placed group-level effect is more efficient because it reduces the number of processed channels. Use the mixer to expose parameters to script so you can animate cutoff frequency, wet/dry gains, or effect send levels dynamically. When designing, think in groups — music, SFX, dialogue — so you can tune each channel independently and snapshot them together. Always test the audible impact and observe mixer VU meters to avoid clipping. Practical control of these parameters gives you real-time expressive power over the entire soundscape. Audio Mixer Effects means apply effects at group level to change many sounds at once and expose parameters to script for runtime control.. In practical terms, common effects you’ll use and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Audio Mixer Effects
Common Effects
  • Reverb — simulates room reflections and decay.
  • Echo / Delay — creates repeats and slapback for depth.
  • Distortion / Chorus / Flange — alter timbre for special moments.
  • Lowpass / Highpass Filters — sculpt frequency ranges for occlusion or underwater.
Design approach
Organize groups like Music, SFX, Dialogue and attach appropriate effects to each so global changes are manageable.
Example
To make the whole game sound muffled underwater, add a Lowpass filter to Master or SFX group, expose the cutoff frequency, and animate it down to about 500Hz in the underwater snapshot. This changes all routed clips without altering source assets.
Expose Parameters
Right-click a parameter in the mixer and expose it to script so your code can set cutoff or wet/dry values at runtime.
Key Takeaway

Applying effects on mixer groups and exposing parameters to script is the most scalable way to change audio behavior at runtime.

screens.title: Snapshots & TransitionToSnapshot
screens.narratorSegment: Audio Mixer Snapshots are saved parameter states that let you change multiple mix properties in one operation. In practice you create snapshots like Normal and Underwater in the mixer, configure group volumes and exposed filter values, and then call TransitionTo on the snapshot to smoothly reach that state. The manager script pattern in the chapter shows fields for the mixer and the snapshots and simple methods like SetUnderwaterAudioState that call TransitionTo with a transition time. This approach avoids iterating over many sources and keeps your runtime logic compact. For example, on entering an underwater trigger, call underwaterSnapshot. TransitionTo(1.0) to lower volumes and reduce cutoff over one second. A misconception is to try to animate every Audio Source separately; snapshots are designed for synchronized global changes. When you need finer control, expose parameters on groups and set them directly with mainMixer. SetFloat for individual knobs. In short, snapshots provide an efficient, game-friendly A P I for expressive audio states. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Snapshots & TransitionToSnapshot
Code Example
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Audio;

public class AudioStateController : MonoBehaviour
{
    public AudioMixer mainMixer;
    public AudioMixerSnapshot normalSnapshot;
    public AudioMixerSnapshot underwaterSnapshot;
    public float transitionTime = 1.0f;

    void Start()
    {
        if (normalSnapshot != null) normalSnapshot.TransitionTo(0.01f);
    }

    public void EnterUnderwater()
    {
        if (underwaterSnapshot != null) underwaterSnapshot.TransitionTo(transitionTime);
    }

    public void ExitUnderwater()
    {
        if (normalSnapshot != null) normalSnapshot.TransitionTo(transitionTime);
    }
}
This pattern centralizes state transitions and keeps runtime calls simple and declarative.
Example Usage
Assign snapshots in the Inspector, place trigger volumes, and call EnterUnderwater from OnTriggerEnter. The entire mix transitions smoothly without modifying individual sources.
Pro-tip
Use short transition times for UI changes and longer times for environmental shifts to maintain immersion.
Key Takeaway

Snapshots let you change the whole audio mix atomically, which is efficient and consistent for gameplay-driven transitions.

screens.title: Audio Clip Settings & Import Choices
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right audio import settings affects memory and C P U. For long music tracks use Streaming so Unity streams samples from disk rather than keeping the whole clip in memory. For shorter clips you often choose compressed Vorbis to reduce file size while keeping reasonable quality. For very short, frequently played SFX, Decompress On Load with PCM can be faster at runtime because it avoids per-play decompression costs, at the expense of using more memory. A common misconception is that maximum compression always saves C P U; in fact heavy runtime decompression can cost C P U and cause spikes when many clips play. The rule of thumb: stream long ambient or music files, compress medium assets, and keep very short, high-frequency clips decompressed if memory allows. Always measure in your target environment. Also pay attention to sample rates and stereo vs mono; converting to mono when appropriate halves the channel data and reduces C P U. These choices are crucial when designing many simultaneous sounds or when targeting constrained platforms. Audio Clip Settings & Import Choices means stream long tracks, compress medium assets, and decompress short, frequently used sfx when memory allows to reduce runtime cost.. In practical terms, streaming, compression, and decompression trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Audio Clip Settings & Import Choices
Options
  • Streaming: Stream long clips from disk to save memory.
  • Vorbis compression: Good balance of size and quality for most files.
  • Decompress On Load (PCM): Lower runtime CPU for short, frequent sounds at memory cost.
Decision checklist
Consider clip length, play frequency, memory budget, and platform I/O when choosing import settings.
Example
A 3-minute ambient track should be Streaming. Short footstep sounds should be Decompress On Load if they play many times per second and your memory allows it. If you must optimize further, convert true mono sources to mono in the import settings.
Key Takeaway

Balance memory and CPU: streaming for long files, decompressed short assets for minimal runtime cost, and compressed medium files to save storage.

screens.title: Audio Source Culling & Bypass Options
screens.narratorSegment: Unity automatically culls Audio Sources based on distance and audibility, but you should tune Max Distance and rolloff curves to match your intended behavior. Reducing Max Distance prevents inaudible sources from consuming processing time. Additionally the Audio Source component has Bypass Effects and Bypass Listener Effects toggles. If a particular sound never needs group effects or listener processing, enabling bypass saves a small amount of C P U per source because the mixer path is simplified. A misconception is that bypassing everything always saves a lot; it saves marginally and should be used when appropriate. Use culling together with prioritized playback: make important sounds have higher priority and ensure that less important ones can be skipped under budget constraints. Test scenarios with many simultaneous sounds and observe how culling affects perceived audio. Keep in mind that too aggressive culling can make the world feel silent at range; tune for the intended player experience rather than purely technical reduction. In practical terms, managing source processing cost in large scenes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Audio Source Culling & Bypass
Culling

Set Max Distance appropriately and choose rolloff curves that match how loud you want a source to be at range. Unity will stop updating sources past audibility thresholds to save work.

Prioritization
Mark critical sounds with higher priority and allow non-critical ones to be culled when many sounds play simultaneously.
Bypass Options
Use Bypass Effects and Bypass Listener Effects to eliminate unnecessary mixer processing on known clean sources.
Example & Test
If a distant ambient insect loop is barely audible, lower its Max Distance or reduce its volume and let the mixer handle the rest. In a stress test with many gunshots, check the Profiler for Audio.Update spikes and adjust culling and prioritization accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Culling and bypass flags are small but essential levers for keeping audio CPU predictable in dense scenes.

screens.title: Object Pooling for SFX
screens.narratorSegment: Instantiating and destroying GameObjects with Audio Sources each time a sound plays is a common source of performance spikes and garbage collection. The recommended pattern is object pooling: pre-instantiate a set of Audio Source GameObjects at scene start and reuse them. When a sound needs to play, grab a free pooled Audio Source, set its clip, position, and volume, call Play or PlayOneShot depending on overlap needs, and return it to the pool when the clip finishes. This reduces runtime allocation and spreads cost into startup rather than gameplay. Be careful to size the pool for expected concurrency and provide overflow handling—either expand the pool up to a limit or skip lower-priority sounds when exhausted. For example, for weapon firing create a pool of a dozen sources; when many bullets fire, reuse them instead of instantiating transient objects each frame. A typical mistake is pooling without resetting transform or parameters, which can lead to lingering positions or volumes. Reset each pooled item's state before reuse and consider using a lightweight timer to release sources automatically when playback ends. Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Object Pooling for SFX
Architecture

Pooling System

Pool Lifecycle
  1. Pre-instantiate pool at startup with N Audio Source objects.
  2. On play request, take a free source and configure clip and transform.
  3. Play and monitor completion; when done, reset and return to pool.
Sizing & Overflow
Pick pool size to cover expected concurrent sounds. On overflow either expand to a cap or skip low-priority sounds to remain stable.
Common pitfalls
  • Not resetting position, volume, pitch, and routing when reusing an Audio Source.
  • Mismatched pool size causing unintended sound drops or overflow allocations.
Key Takeaway

Pooling moves allocation cost out of tight gameplay loops and reduces GC pressure, keeping audio performance smooth under load.

screens.title: PlayOneShot() vs Play() and Mixing Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between AudioSource. PlayOneShot and AudioSource. Play affects overlap and resource usage. PlayOneShot plays a clip on the source without stopping any currently playing clip on that source, which is ideal for overlapping, short SFX like multiple gunshots or rapid footsteps. Play stops any existing clip on that Audio Source and starts the assigned clip, which is useful when a single logical source should not produce overlapping sounds. If you need simultaneous instances from the same logical emitter, use multiple AudioSource components or a pooled system instead of repeatedly calling Play to avoid cutting sounds prematurely. A common misconception is that PlayOneShot always costs less; under heavy overlapping it can still increase mixing load because multiple voices are active. Balance overlap needs with prioritization and pooling. For music and long-form audio, use dedicated Music mixer groups with crossfading between sources or snapshots for global transitions. Designing a clear routing strategy—Music, SFX, Dialogue—lets you control levels and effects independently and avoids confusing interactions. PlayOneShot()

Ideal for overlapping short effects. It does not stop the currently playing clip on the Audio Source, allowing multiple instances to mix together.

Use when
Multiple quick events like rapid gunfire or footsteps that should overlap.
Play()

Stops the source's current clip and starts the assigned clip. Use when the logical emitter should only produce one sound at a time.

Use when
Single-shot emitters like a radio that should not layer multiple audio events.
Key Takeaway

Match your playback API to overlap requirements: PlayOneShot for overlap, Play for exclusive playback, and pools or multiple sources when you need many simultaneous voices from one logical emitter.

screens.title: Dynamic Music Systems
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic music systems change the musical backdrop to match gameplay intensity. The chapter outlines three common techniques. Layering plays multiple stems on separate Audio Sources routed to a Music group; you fade stems in or out to change intensity without restarting music. Stingers are short musical phrases played once to accent an event, then you return to the main music. Crossfading moves between distinct tracks or variations smoothly, often using snapshots or scripted volume automation. For example, when combat starts fade in the percussion stem while lowering the calm exploration stem; if the player defeats a boss, play a stinger and transition to a victory snapshot. A misconception is that music must stop to change mood; well-designed layering avoids audible jumps and preserves musical continuity. Use the Audio Mixer to route music stems and create snapshots for master-level changes like EQ, reverb, or global volume. Test transitions in context to ensure musical phrases line up and that crossfades do not clash rhythmically or harmonically. screens.title: Profiling & Troubleshooting Audio
screens.narratorSegment: Profiling is essential when advanced audio features and many concurrent sounds meet limited C P U budgets. Use Unity's Profiler under Window > Analysis > Profiler and observe Audio. Update and Audio. ProcessEffects counters. If you see spikes when entering a new area, check for many simultaneous sources, heavy per-source effects, or large numbers of decompressions. The Audio Mixer VU meters help you spot clipping and level inconsistencies; ensure Master and group meters don’t peak. When you find a hotspot, apply targeted fixes: reduce concurrent voices with pooling or culling, route heavy processing into group-level effects instead of per-source, or adjust clip import settings to minimize runtime decompression. A common troubleshooting step is to mute groups one-by-one to isolate which group contributes most to load. Also verify that exposed parameters are routed correctly and that snapshots are saved. Always test on the target hardware because desktop profiling can differ from consoles or mobile. The final practical habit is to iterate: measure, change one variable, and re-measure until acceptable performance is achieved. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we bridge audio design and performance engineering so your game sounds immersive and runs smoothly. You will learn how to create believable spatial audio using zones and occlusion, shape sound with the Audio Mixer and snapshots, and build systems that adapt music and effects to gameplay. We also cover practical optimization: choosing clip settings, culling audio sources, and using object pooling to avoid costly instantiation. Each idea ties back to a real requirement: players expect believable sound placement, seamless transitions between audio states, and consistent performance across platforms. For example, an underwater snapshot uses a low-pass filter and reduced volumes to sell immersion without changing every clip. A common mistake is adjusting dozens of sources instead of using mixer snapshots; the snapshot approach lets you change the whole mix smoothly and efficiently. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to implement snapshot transitions, add occlusion, and profile audio C P U usage so sounds are both convincing and cost-effective. Think about which audio problem in your project matters most, and we’ll address it step by step.

These objectives focus on four core competencies you will practice. First, implement advanced spatial audio techniques so sounds feel like they come from real places; you will use zones and occlusion, and learn why a low-pass filter can simulate being behind a wall or underwater. Second, apply Audio Mixer effects and snapshots to create dynamic audio states; snapshots let you change many parameters at once, which is essential for efficient global transitions. Third, optimize audio performance through clip settings, audio culling, and object pooling so your C P U stays predictable when many sounds play. Fourth, design dynamic music that reacts to gameplay by layering tracks, using stingers, and crossfading with mixer transitions. Each objective connects to hands-on steps: expose filter parameters, create snapshots, tag trigger zones, and implement a pool for reusable Audio Sources. As you learn, compare common mistakes like changing dozens of clips directly instead of driving a mixer snapshot, and practice using the Profiler to measure audio cost. Aim to leave with practical code patterns and an ability to choose the right audio tool for both fidelity and performance.

These additional objectives emphasize practical setup and problem solving. First, implement an audio snapshot system that transitions states programmatically, for example switching to an "Underwater" snapshot when the player submerges. Second, set up trigger volumes and script entry/exit handlers so gameplay events reliably drive audio state changes. Third, learn to profile audio performance using Unity's Profiler to find costly Audio. Update calls or expensive effects, and use the mixer's meters to prevent clipping and distortion. Fourth, troubleshoot common audio issues by checking routing, exposed parameters, and clip import settings. Each objective includes a hands-on step: expose the low-pass cutoff, build a trigger zone with a boxed collider set to trigger, attach a small controller script, and verify transitions in Play Mode. A frequent misconception is thinking changing every Audio Source is necessary for a global effect; snapshots and mixer groups are the intended, scalable solution. Practicing these objectives will make your audio both robust and maintainable.

Spatial audio is the perception that a sound comes from a particular place in 3D space, including its direction and distance. When you set Spatial Blend to full 3D you get basic positional cues, but true environmental realism comes from audio zones and reverb. An Audio Reverb Zone applies a reverb effect to any audio that plays inside its collider, simulating a cave, hall, or small room without changing the source clips. For example, place an Audio Reverb Zone inside a cavern and tune the reverb decay and wet level; footsteps and distant echoes will suddenly feel correct. A common misconception is to bake reverb into clips or duplicate clips per area; this becomes hard to manage. Using zones keeps source clips clean and lets you adjust acoustics globally. In practice you will combine zones with 3D rolloff curves and Max Distance to control how sources fade. As you test, listen for sudden jumps when crossing zone boundaries; smoothing or overlapping zones can avoid audible pops. Consider how music and dialogue thread through these spaces so the player experiences a consistent sound field. What space in your level would benefit most from a reverb zone?

Occlusion and obstruction simulate how objects affect sound reaching the listener. Occlusion mutes or muffles a source when a complete or substantial barrier exists between listener and source. Obstruction models partial blocking, reducing high frequencies and slightly lowering volume. A common implementation starts with a raycast from the Audio Listener to the Audio Source. If the ray hits geometry, you treat it as occluded and adjust parameters—typically reduce volume and increase low-pass filtering. For partial hits or multiple rays, blend between unobstructed and obstructed states to avoid popping. For example, when the player stands behind a thin wall, apply a mild low-pass cutoff at around 2000 to 5000 hertz and reduce volume by a few decibels; for a concrete wall you may drop the cutoff lower and attenuate more. Remember that precise numbers depend on the game's sonic design. Test with music and SFX to ensure speech remains intelligible when intended. A misconception is using only distance rolloff; occlusion requires additional geometry checks to sound believable. The final step is smoothing parameter changes over time so transitions feel natural rather than abrupt.

The Audio Mixer is Unity's central tool for grouping audio and applying effects. Each group can host effects such as Reverb, Echo, Distortion, Chorus, Flange, Delay, and lowpass/highpass filters. These effects change the character of sounds in ways that are expensive to simulate per-source but economical when done on groups. For instance, applying a low-pass filter to the SFX group can make all group sounds behave as if heard through water or behind a wall. A frequent misconception is assuming that effects on the master group are always cheaper; sometimes a well-placed group-level effect is more efficient because it reduces the number of processed channels. Use the mixer to expose parameters to script so you can animate cutoff frequency, wet/dry gains, or effect send levels dynamically. When designing, think in groups — music, SFX, dialogue — so you can tune each channel independently and snapshot them together. Always test the audible impact and observe mixer VU meters to avoid clipping. Practical control of these parameters gives you real-time expressive power over the entire soundscape. Audio Mixer Effects means apply effects at group level to change many sounds at once and expose parameters to script for runtime control.. In practical terms, common effects you’ll use and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Audio Mixer Snapshots are saved parameter states that let you change multiple mix properties in one operation. In practice you create snapshots like Normal and Underwater in the mixer, configure group volumes and exposed filter values, and then call TransitionTo on the snapshot to smoothly reach that state. The manager script pattern in the chapter shows fields for the mixer and the snapshots and simple methods like SetUnderwaterAudioState that call TransitionTo with a transition time. This approach avoids iterating over many sources and keeps your runtime logic compact. For example, on entering an underwater trigger, call underwaterSnapshot. TransitionTo(1.0) to lower volumes and reduce cutoff over one second. A misconception is to try to animate every Audio Source separately; snapshots are designed for synchronized global changes. When you need finer control, expose parameters on groups and set them directly with mainMixer. SetFloat for individual knobs. In short, snapshots provide an efficient, game-friendly A P I for expressive audio states. Choosing the right audio import settings affects memory and C P U. For long music tracks use Streaming so Unity streams samples from disk rather than keeping the whole clip in memory. For shorter clips you often choose compressed Vorbis to reduce file size while keeping reasonable quality. For very short, frequently played SFX, Decompress On Load with PCM can be faster at runtime because it avoids per-play decompression costs, at the expense of using more memory. A common misconception is that maximum compression always saves C P U; in fact heavy runtime decompression can cost C P U and cause spikes when many clips play. The rule of thumb: stream long ambient or music files, compress medium assets, and keep very short, high-frequency clips decompressed if memory allows. Always measure in your target environment. Also pay attention to sample rates and stereo vs mono; converting to mono when appropriate halves the channel data and reduces C P U. Choosing between AudioSource. PlayOneShot and AudioSource. Play affects overlap and resource usage. PlayOneShot plays a clip on the source without stopping any currently playing clip on that source, which is ideal for overlapping, short SFX like multiple gunshots or rapid footsteps.
